title: Village Walks and Day Hikes Around Kalimpong
meta_description: Eight day walks around Kalimpong, Lava, Rishyap, Sillery Gaon, Pedong and Lolegaon: distances, times, height gain, guides, leeches and safety.
summary: The best walking around Kalimpong is on village paths, not long treks: Lava to Rishyap through forest (about 4 km, 400 m up), dawn at Tiffin Dara, Ramitey Dara from Sillery Gaon (3 km), Damsang fort from Pedong, Lolegaon's canopy walk and the 5 km stroll down from Deolo. Most take one to three hours; guides cost ₹600–1,000.

sections.heading: How walking works in these hills
paras: There are no multi-day trekking routes with huts in Kalimpong district the way there are on the Singalila Ridge. What there is, in every direction, is a web of village paths: short cuts between hamlets, forest tracks to viewpoints, and old mule roads that predate the motor road. Locals use them daily, and most of the best views in the district are a 20-minute to two-hour walk from where the car stops.

That shapes how we plan. Base yourself in a homestay village for two nights, walk one route at dawn and another in the afternoon, and let your hosts point you to the right path. Mornings from 6 to 10 am give the clearest views and the steadiest weather; by early afternoon cloud often fills the valleys. The best months are October to December and March to May. In the monsoon, from June to September, paths are slippery, leeches are everywhere, and views are rare.

sections.heading: The walks at a glance
paras: Distances and times are one way unless marked, for a steady walker with stops; heights are approximate. Add 30–50% if you walk with children or older parents, or stop often for photographs and birds.

sections.heading: Lava to Rishyap, and Tiffin Dara
paras: This is the finest forest walk in the district. From Lava at about 2,200 m, a path climbs roughly 4 km through oak, rhododendron and bamboo to Rishyap at 2,591 m, a gain of about 400 m that takes most people 2–2.5 hours. The road between the two is 10 km, so the path is the local short cut. In March and April the rhododendrons flower along the upper half; in any dry month you will hear mixed flocks of birds moving through the trees.

Many travellers send their bags ahead by car, about ₹800–1,200, and walk up light. Go with a local guide or someone from your homestay the first time: there are side paths, and mist can close in within minutes. Next morning, walk the 1 km from Rishyap to Tiffin Dara in the dark with a torch and be there 20 minutes before sunrise. On a clear day the Kanchenjunga range lights up from end to end.

sections.heading: Sillery Gaon and the bends of the Teesta
paras: Sillery Gaon, at about 1,830 m above Pedong, has one walk everyone does: Ramitey Dara, about 3 km away. The path runs along the ridge through forest and fields with some ups and downs, about 1–1.5 hours each way. From the top, the Teesta is seen making 14 bends far below (some people count 11), with Kanchenjunga above on a clear morning. Go early; the valley fills with haze by late morning, and the bends vanish first.

Homestay hosts in Sillery Gaon often send a young family member as a guide for a few hundred rupees. Settle the fee before you start. A car can also take you most of the way, but the walk is the better half of the experience.

sections.heading: Damsang fort from Pedong or Icchey Gaon
paras: The ruins of Damsang Gadi, the fort of the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok, lie on a ridge 2–3 km from Pedong. It was built in the late 17th century (1690 is often quoted) to resist the Bhutanese, and fell to ruin after 1864. Lepcha lore says spirits carried smooth round stones from the Reshi river to build its walls; the local guides tell it as a story, not history. Little stands today but low stone walls among trees, which is part of the appeal.

From Pedong the walk takes about an hour; from Icchey Gaon it is about 6 km, a half-day out and back through village paths and forest. Take water and a snack, as there are no shops on the way. On 20 December, Lepchas gather at the fort for Gaeboo Achyok's birth anniversary; if you visit then, keep to the edges and ask before photographing anyone.

sections.heading: Kolakham and Lolegaon
paras: Changey Falls is about 4 km from Kolakham by road, and from the roadhead a path of about 900 m leads down to the fall. Going down takes 20–30 minutes; coming back up is the harder part, so pace yourself. After rain the stones are slick, and in the monsoon the fall is at its fullest but the path is at its worst.

Lolegaon's heritage forest has a canopy walk: a hanging bridge of about 180 m strung through old oak and cypress, with a short path around it. It is level and easy, but not for anyone uneasy with height or sway. Jhandi Dara, 4–5 km from the village, is Lolegaon's sunrise point; walk it with a torch before dawn, or take a local car up and walk back down after sunrise. Kafer viewpoint, about 1 km away, is the easy evening stroll.

sections.heading: Deolo down to Dr Graham's Homes
paras: The gentlest walk on this list starts at the top of Deolo hill, at 1,704 m the highest point of Kalimpong, with its Science Centre and paragliding take-off. From there, walk about 5 km down through the slopes to Dr Graham's Homes, the school founded in 1900, at the foot of the hill. It is mostly downhill on road and paths, about 1.5–2 hours with stops, and ends near enough to town for a short taxi ride back. Do it on a weekday afternoon after a morning at Durpin, and ask at the school gate before walking the campus roads.

sections.heading: Safety, leeches and guides
paras: None of these walks is technical, but hill paths still catch people out every season. These are the rules we give our own travellers:
list: Hire a local guide for the Lava–Rishyap path, Damsang fort and Jhandi Dara the first time; expect ₹600–1,000 for a day, less for a short walk
Tell your homestay where you are going and when you expect to be back
Start by 7 am, and turn back by early afternoon, when mist and rain usually arrive
Carry a torch for dawn walks, 1 litre of water each, a rain shell and a warm layer
From May to October wear leech socks or tuck trousers into long socks; remove leeches with salt, never by pulling
Wear shoes with real grip; moss-covered stones are slippery even in dry weeks
Mobile signal comes and goes on ridges and in forest, so do not rely on online maps
Neora Valley National Park needs a permit and a registered guide from Lava; check current status before you travel

faqs.q: Can we walk from Lava to Rishyap?
faqs.a: Yes. A forest path of about 4 km climbs roughly 400 m from Lava to Rishyap and takes most walkers 2–2.5 hours. The road between them is 10 km. Go with a local guide or someone from your homestay the first time, because side paths branch off and mist can close in quickly. Send bags ahead by car for about ₹800–1,200.

faqs.q: How far is Tiffin Dara from Rishyap?
faqs.a: Tiffin Dara is about 1 km from Rishyap village, a 20–30 minute walk with a short climb at the end. Leave in the dark with a torch and arrive about 20 minutes before sunrise. On a clear morning, most reliable from October to December, the full Kanchenjunga range is visible. Carry a warm layer, as Rishyap sits at 2,591 m.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to Ramitey Dara from Sillery Gaon?
faqs.a: Ramitey Dara is about 3 km from Sillery Gaon, around 1–1.5 hours each way along a ridge path with some ups and downs. From the top the Teesta is seen making 14 bends (some count 11). Go early, before late-morning haze hides the river, and settle any guide fee with your homestay before you start.

faqs.q: How do we get to Damsang fort?
faqs.a: The Damsang fort ruins are 2–3 km from Pedong, about an hour's walk, or about 6 km from Icchey Gaon, a half-day out and back. The fort belonged to the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok and dates from the late 17th century. Little remains but low stone walls among trees. Carry water, as there are no shops along the way.

faqs.q: Is the Changey Falls walk difficult?
faqs.a: Not very. From the roadhead, about 4 km from Kolakham, a path of roughly 900 m leads down to the falls in 20–30 minutes. The climb back up is the harder part, so take it slowly. Stones are slippery after rain, and in the monsoon the path is at its worst even though the fall is at its fullest.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for walks around Kalimpong?
faqs.a: For short walks like Tiffin Dara, Kafer viewpoint or the Deolo descent, no. For the Lava–Rishyap forest path, Damsang fort and Jhandi Dara, a local guide is wise the first time, at about ₹600–1,000 a day or less for a short walk. Neora Valley National Park always needs a registered guide; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there leeches on Kalimpong walks?
faqs.a: Yes, from about May to October leeches are common on forest paths, especially around Lava, Rishyap, Kolakham and Lolegaon. They are harmless but unpleasant. Wear leech socks or tuck trousers into long socks, check your ankles often, and remove them with salt. From November to April most paths are almost free of them.

faqs.q: What is the best season for day hikes near Kalimpong?
faqs.a: October to December, for dry paths and clear mountain views, followed by March to May, when rhododendrons flower on the Lava–Rishyap path and birds are singing. January and February are cold but clear, with snow some years at Lava and Rishyap. From June to September rain, landslides and leeches make walking slow and views rare.

faqs.q: Is the Lolegaon canopy walk safe?
faqs.a: It is a hanging bridge of about 180 m through old oak and cypress in Lolegaon's heritage forest, built for visitors and easy underfoot. It sways, so people uneasy with height may not enjoy it, and small children should be held. Rules on numbers and timings are set by the forest department; check current status before you travel.
